# Now

> "Therefore don't be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day's own evil is sufficient."
>
> — Matthew 6:34

You've reached the last chapter. I'm glad you came all the way.

Congratulations. I mean that as plainly as I can say it. You were caught in something that holds most men for life, and you walked out. You'll discover over the coming months that life was better than you thought it was. The habit had been standing in front of it.

## Today is the only day you've got {-}

One more idea before you go. It's short, and it'll serve you long after you've forgotten the rest.

The habit lived in two places, and neither was real. It lived in the past: the shame of last night, the tally of broken promises. And it lived in the future: "How will I manage a whole lifetime without it?" Nobody can manage a lifetime. A lifetime doesn't arrive in one piece. It comes one ordinary day at a time, and no man has ever had to stay free on any day except this one.

Jesus told his friends the same thing. Leave tomorrow alone, because it has worries enough of its own. Yesterday is confessed and finished with. Tomorrow isn't yours yet. What you've been given is this afternoon.

So here is something to practise. Soon, perhaps this week, a thought will float up: "I could, just now." A second later you'll catch it and think, "That's not me. It's the leftover noise of a thing I've finished with." Then you'll feel a small burst of gladness that the thought no longer gives you orders. That's another kind of moment of revelation, and you can have it as often as you like.

It works on other thoughts too. Take the grumble on the drive to work, the replayed argument, or the worry at three in the morning. A thought is something that passes through your head. You are not the thought, and you needn't salute it. A man can sit on a beach at sunset with everything he ever asked for and be wretched because of what's going on in his head. Another man can be in a traffic jam in the rain and be perfectly content.

If you're a Christian, you have the better half of this. You don't just watch your thoughts go by. You hand them over. If you're not a believer, the watching half is still yours: notice the thought, name it, let it pass. It works all the same.

Right now, as you read, nothing is wrong. You're free, you're forgiven, and you're breathing. Start from there, and start from there again tomorrow.

## So where to now? {-}

Don't rebuild your life around having stopped. I've said it before and this is the last time: a man who rearranges his whole existence to keep away from a thing is still living in its shadow. Go on with your life as it was.

All the same, something has changed. You have a cleared space. You've got back the hours, the energy and the attention that the habit used to eat. An empty room doesn't stay empty for long, so decide what goes in it.

Thomas Chalmers, the old Scottish preacher you met in Chapter 20, asked about the heart's old attachment: "may it not be supplanted by the love of that which is more worthy than itself?" It may. Stopping was never the whole point. A greater love now has room to move in.

For a Christian that means God first: not as a guard posted at the door, but as the one you were made to enjoy. Pray like a man with nothing to hide, because you have nothing to hide. Open the Bible because you want to. Sit in church without the old feeling of being a fraud in a pew.

For any man it means the people in front of you. Your wife, who gets the whole of you now. Your children, who get a father who isn't half elsewhere. Your friends and your work, and the thing you always meant to build.

Remember the thread that has run through this book from the first page: a man who can't control his lust can't be trusted. You've become a man who can. People will start to lean on you without quite knowing why. Let them.

## Pass it on {-}

This book is free. It always will be. Nobody is selling you a course, an app, a coaching call or a second volume. It's released under an open licence, which means you may copy it, print it, translate it, quote it and hand it round without asking anyone. The Attribution page has the details.

It's free because it was given to us. The method came from Allen Carr. The people behind EasyPeasy reworked it and gave it away. We took their gift, applied it to this habit, and are giving it away in turn. Jesus put the principle in one short sentence when he sent his disciples out: "Freely you received, so freely give."

So there's no bill. But if this book has done you good, I'll ask one thing of you: pay it forward.

Augustine was a grown man, weeping under a fig tree over his own "not yet", when he heard a child's voice from the house next door chanting, "Take up and read; Take up and read." He picked up the book beside him, and the long fight ended that afternoon. The child never knew what it had done.

You can be that voice for someone, and it takes very little.

- **Tell one man.** Somebody came to mind while you were reading. It might be a brother, a friend, or a lad at church. Send him the link with one line: "This worked for me."
- **Share it where men are struggling.** When you see someone online grinding through his fourth streak of the year, point him here, kindly, and leave it at that.
- **Give it to those who lead men.** Your pastor, your youth leader, the chap who runs the men's group.
- **Make it better.** The text is open. If you find a mistake, a clumsy sentence or a better illustration, send it in. If you speak another language, translate it.
- **Send them to the parent book as well.** Any man still tangled in porn needs [EasyPeasy](https://easypeasymethod.org/) too.

Don't preach it and don't argue it. You know by now that nobody is argued out of this trap. Pass the book along and get on with your day. The men who need it will read it at one in the morning, on their own, the way you probably did.

## A blessing {-}

I don't know your name, and you don't know mine. But I've thought about you through every chapter, and I'd like to end by praying for you. These are the oldest words of blessing I know. If you're an atheist, play along one last time, and take it as a stranger wishing you well with his whole heart.

> "Yahweh bless you, and keep you.
>
> Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you.
>
> Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace."
>
> — Numbers 6:24-26

You're free. Go and live like it, and bring somebody with you.

Yours,

AnotherHackAuthor
